_comment: Hindu expansion part 3: epic episodes cut per story (Yayati, Savitri, Skanda's birth, Yudhishthira's ascension, Sita's fire trial). All passages are paraphrases of public-domain translations.

region.en: Pratishthana on the Ganges, Yayati's capital (symbolic pin near Prayagraj)
region.zh: 恆河畔耶耶提都城缽哩沙陀那（象徵性定位近般遮羅闍）

texts.period: Mahabharata, Adi Parva (Sharmishtha Upaparva), composition layers c. 400 BCE-400 CE (Ganguli translation, 1883-96)

source.work: The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, trans. K. M. Ganguli (1883-96), Adi Parva, the story of Yayati

summary.en: Cursed by his father-in-law to age before his time, the emperor Yayati begs each of his sons to trade him their youth. Four sons of Devayani refuse; his youngest, born of the servant Sharmishtha, agrees - and Yayati spends a thousand years of borrowed youth chasing pleasure, only to discover that desire is never satisfied by feeding it. He returns the youth, renounces the throne, and goes into the forest.
summary.zh: 耶耶提遭岳父之詛提前衰老，乞求諸子與之交易青春。德瓦亞尼所生四子皆拒；侍女沙爾蜜什陀所生之幼子應允——耶耶提以借來的千年青春追逐歡樂，終悟欲望愈餵愈飽不得。他歸還青春、放棄王位、入林而去。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition (epic recitation; katha retellings). Classified 'myth'.

passages.text: Devayani, daughter of the sage Shukra, married King Yayati in anger at the princess Sharmishtha; Sharmishtha followed her as a servant and bore Yayati secret sons. When Shukra learned of the union, his curse fell: Yayati would pass into old age, untimely, deprived of his pleasures in the prime of life.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Yayati episode (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

passages.text: Old age came upon the emperor like a guest he could not turn away. He went to his sons, each in turn: take my old age upon you, he said, and give me your youth, that I may enjoy the world a while longer and then hand it back. Four sons of Devayani refused - who would take a spent man's years for their own spring? Only Puru, the youngest, son of the servant, said: take it, father; I will bear your age and stand by your word.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Yayati episode (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

passages.text: With Puru's youth upon him Yayati resumed the pleasures of the senses - the gardens, the women, the hunts, the feasts - a thousand years of it, and every appetite only grew the more it was fed. At last he understood: desire is like fire; it is never satisfied by fuel. 'There is no end to desire,' he said; 'he who feeds it starves by feeding.' He gave Puru back his youth, declared Puru heir - disinheriting the elder line - and went to the forest with nothing, eating leaves, desiring nothing.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Yayati episode (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: Kisari Mohan Ganguli, The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, 1883-96 (public domain); modern: J. A. B. van Buitenen, The Mahabharata, vol. 1, University of Chicago Press, 1973

narrative.en:
The story of Yayati, told in the Adi Parva as part of the genealogy of kings, is the Mahabharata's sharpest fable about desire - and the charter myth of the Puru dynasty, the line from which the epic's own Bharata kings descend.

The tangle begins in a household war. Devayani, daughter of the preceptor Shukra, is humiliated by the Asura princess Sharmishtha and thrown into a well; Yayati rescues her; she marries him on condition that Sharmishtha be given to her as a servant. But Sharmishtha, in the palace as a maid, is soon secretly Yayati's mistress too, and bears him sons. When Shukra learns of it, his curse is precise and domestic: Yayati shall pass into untimely old age, cheated of his pleasures at their height.

The curse is also the experiment. Old age arrives, and Yayati - not yet done with the world - goes to his sons with the strangest request in the epic: give me your youth and carry my old age; I will enjoy the world a while and return what I borrow. The four sons of Devayani refuse, with the eldest speaking for them: what wise man would trade his springtime for another's winter? Only Puru, the youngest, son of the servant Sharmishtha - the unprivileged son - consents: 'take it, father; I will bear your age and stand by your word.'

So armed, Yayati re-enters the world's pleasures for a thousand years - the text lingers on the inventory: gardens, women, hunting, wine, festivity. And the experiment's result is the story's entire point: a thousand years of feeding desire leaves it hungrier, not quieter. Yayati's conclusion is spoken like a scientist closing his notebook: desire is a fire that no fuel satisfies; 'he who feeds it starves by feeding'; there is no end of wanting, only an end of the wanting man. He returns Puru's youth, makes Puru his heir - disinheriting the elder sons and founding the line of Puru that leads, in the epic's genealogy, to Bharata and to the Pandavas themselves - and walks into the forest owning nothing, 'desiring nothing, eating leaves and fruit'. The curse thus becomes a cure: the father-in-law's punishment delivers the hero to renunciation by the longest possible route.

Function: the story is recited as a teaching fable on craving (the epic's own frame commentary calls it the story of how even a thousand years of indulgence teaches only one sentence) and as a legitimation myth - the youngest servant-born son becomes the dynasty's founder because he alone paid his father's debt. In later retellings (Purana versions; Marathi and modern novel treatments, e.g. Vishnu Sakharam Khandekar's Yayati), the emphasis shifts between the erotic fable and the dynastic politics - the servant queen's line displacing the high-born one, a troubling undercurrent the epic leaves unresolved.
narrative.zh: 耶耶提的故事見於阿底篇王統之中，是摩訶婆羅多關於欲望最鋒利的寓言——也是補魯王朝的創建神話，史詩自身的婆羅多王族即出此系。家庭之戰開其端：仙人尸 訶之女德瓦亞尼受阿修羅公主沙爾蜜什陀之辱而墮井；耶耶提救之；她以沙爾蜜什陀為婢為條件嫁之。然沙爾蜜什陀居宮為婢，旋為耶耶提之秘密情人，生子數人。尸訶得知，其詛精確而家常：耶耶提將提前衰老，於歡樂正盛時被剝奪。詛咒亦即實驗。衰老降臨，耶耶提——未厭於世——向諸子提出史詩中最奇異的請求：予我青春而代我衰老；我將稍享世界而歸還所借。德瓦亞尼四子皆拒，長子代言：孰以己之春換他人之冬？唯侍女之子、最幼者補魯應允：『取之，父；我代父老，守父之言。』耶耶提遂攜補魯之青春重入感官之樂千年——經文細列清單：園林、婦女、田獵、酒宴——而實驗之果即故事全部之義：餵養欲望千年，欲望愈餵愈飢。耶耶提之結論如科學家合上筆記：欲望如火，燃料不能滿之；『餵它者因餵而餓』；欲無盡處，唯有欲者之盡。他歸還補魯之青春，立補魯為嗣——廢長支而建補魯之系，於史詩王統中直達婆羅多與般度諸子——且空手入林，『無所欲，食葉與果』。詛咒遂成療法：岳父之懲罰以最長之路將英雄送至出離。功能：此篇被誦為貪求之教寓言（史詩自註：縱千年之縱慾，所學僅一句），亦為正統神話——侍女所生之幼子因其獨償父債而成王朝之祖。後世重述（往世書；馬拉提語與現代小說，如坎德卡之《耶耶提》）於情欲寓言與王朝政治之間擺動——婢后之支取代嫡支，史詩留下未解的暗流。

functions: Teaching fable on desire: a thousand years of indulgence proves appetite unquenchable
Legitimation myth of the Puru-Bharata dynasty (the servant's son as founder)
Charter of renunciation as the end of the pleasure-path
Genealogical bridge from the gods' era to the epic's own royal line

variants.name: Vishnu Purana version
variants.summary: Condenses the epic telling into dynastic annals, keeping the youth-exchange and Puru's succession; the erotic frame is trimmed to genealogy.

variants.name: Khandekar's Yayati (Marathi, 1959)
variants.summary: Retells the myth from Sharmishtha's and Devayani's perspectives, expanding the women's interiority and making the curse a psychological tragedy rather than a fable.

variants.name: Katha retellings (Puranas and vernacular)
variants.summary: The story circulates as a stand-alone parable in Purana digests and oral katha, often with the moral stated explicitly: the man fed by all the world's pleasures died desiring.

title.en: Savitri Follows Death and Wins Back Her Husband
title.zh: 薩維特里隨死神而奪回夫君

region.en: Forest hermitage of Salva (symbolic pin at Chitrakoot)
region.zh: 薩羅訶王流放之林居（象徵性定位於質多羅俱吒）

texts.period: Mahabharata, Vana Parva (Pativrata Upaparva), composition layers c. 400 BCE-400 CE (Ganguli translation, 1883-96)

source.work: The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, trans. K. M. Ganguli (1883-96), Vana Parva, the story of Savitri and Satyavan

summary.en: Princess Savitri chooses as husband the exiled, doomed Satyavan, despite the seer Narada's prophecy that he will die within a year. On the fated day she follows her husband into the forest and trails Yama himself as he takes Satyavan's soul; her unanswerable courtesy and argument win three boons - and the third is worded so that the fourth, unasked, is his life.
summary.zh: 薩維特里公主不顧那羅陀仙人「夫將於一年內死」之預言，選流放而命定之薩蒂凡為夫。劫日當天，她隨夫入林，並尾隨親自取走薩蒂凡魂魄的閻摩；她以無可辯駁的禮數與言辭赢得三項恩諾——而第三項措辭巧妙，使未出口的第四項成為丈夫之命。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition: the story is ritually recited at Vat-Savitri Vrata (married women's fast). Classified 'myth'.

passages.text: King Ashvapati, childless, worshiped Savitri the sun-goddess with offerings; the goddess granted him a daughter, Savitri, radiant as the sun. When she was of marriageable age, her father sent her to choose - and she returned from the forests having fixed her heart on Satyavan, blind Dyumatsena's son, living in exile at a hermitage.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Savitri episode (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

passages.text: Narada the seer was present, and he pronounced the doom: Satyavan is virtuous beyond all men, but he has one defect - he shall die within a year. The king begged his daughter to choose another; Savitri answered that she had chosen once, for once only, whether he lives one year or more - she has made her choice. The marriage was performed, and she went to the forest, serving her husband's blind parents in homespun.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Savitri episode (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

passages.text: She counted the days. Four days before the term, she began a vigil, standing without food; on the fated day she obtained leave and went with Satyavan to the forest to cut firewood. He felled a tree, grew faint, and lay with his head in her lap; then came a dark-crowned figure with a rope - Yama, Death himself - who drew Satyavan's soul, small as a thumb, and turned south, binding it for the city of the dead.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Savitri episode (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

passages.text: Savitri followed. Yama told her to go back; she kept walking, speaking of duty and of the merit of following. Moved by her discourse, he offered boons: eyes and kingdom for her blind father-in-law; a hundred sons for her father; a hundred sons for herself. He had granted too much: a hundred sons require a living husband. Yama, bound by his own word and outmatched in argument, cut the rope, gave back the soul, and said: your husband shall live. Satyavan woke as from sleep, and the family's fortunes reversed from that day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Savitri episode (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: Kisari Mohan Ganguli, The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, 1883-96 (public domain); modern: S. K. Belvalkar studies; also Julia Leslie's work on the Savitri vrata

narrative.en:
The Savitri episode (Vana Parva, told by Markandeya to Yudhishthira as the story of the perfect wife, pativrata) is the Mahabharata's great love-against-death narrative, and one of the most ritually alive stories in Hinduism: it is recited every year at the Vat-Savitri vrata, the fast married women keep for their husbands' longevity.

The choice: Ashvapati, king of Madra, is childless; he worships the sun-goddess Savitri with disciplined offerings, and she grants him a daughter as radiant as her namesake. When the girl is grown, the king - following custom - sends her on a pilgrimage of self-choice (svayamvara) in a chariot with aged counselors. She travels sanctuaries and hermitages and returns with her heart fixed: on Satyavan, son of the blind exiled king Dyumatsena, living in forest poverty. He is beautiful, dutiful - and doomed.

The oracle: Narada, the celestial seer, happens to be present and delivers the prophecy that gives the story its clock: Satyavan is virtuous beyond all men, but he has one defect - he shall die within a year. The father begs; the daughter's answer is the pivot of the story and the ethic it teaches: 'I have chosen once, whether he lives long or briefly; having chosen, I choose no more.' Death in a year is a defect of fate, not of the man. The marriage is performed with the doom standing, and Savitri goes to the hermitage in homespun, serving her blind parents-in-law.

The vigil: Savitri counts the days inward. Four before the term she begins a standing fast; her father-in-law tries to dissuade her; she answers with theology - the vow is kept, and what will be is known to the wise. On the fated day she obtains leave to go with her husband into the forest. He cuts firewood, faints, and lies with his head in her lap. Then she sees him: a dark-crowned figure carrying a rope, standing as if he owns the wood. It is Yama, and he draws Satyavan's soul - small as a thumb-length - binds it, and turns south toward his city.

The duel: Savitri follows. Yama three times commands her back; three times she stays, and her speeches - on dharma, on the company of the righteous, on the merit of following a husband - are so accomplished that Death himself concedes the conversation. He offers boons to get her to leave: for her father-in-law, eyes and his kingdom restored; for her father, a hundred sons; for herself, a hundred sons. The third boon is the trap she has been building: a hundred sons require a living husband. Yama, bound by his own granted word, laughs and releases the rope. 'Your husband shall live.' Satyavan wakes as from sleep; the exiled family's fortunes reverse; and the seers' prophecy is beaten not by force but by a wife's constancy, timed and worded.

Function: the story is the charter of the pativrata ideal - the devoted wife whose virtue has real cosmological purchase - and the ritual text of Vat-Savitri vrata, in which women fast, tie threads around a banyan, and retell Savitri's argument for their husbands' lives. Sri Aurobindo built his epic Savitri on it; comparative readers place it beside Orpheus (the descent for a wife, failed) and Psyche's tasks - here the descent is refused, and the argument wins where song could not.
narrative.zh: 薩維特里之章（大森林篇，由摩根德耶向堅戰講述，作為貞婦 pativrata 之典範故事）是摩訶婆羅多最偉大的抗死之愛敘事，也是印度教中儀式生命力最強的故事之一：每年 Vat-Savitri 齋戒——已婚婦女為夫壽而持之齋——都誦讀此篇。選擇：摩德羅王苑鏡婆底無子；他以嚴謹的供養禮拜太陽女神薩維特里，女神賜一女，光輝如其名。女長，王依俗遣其自擇夫婿（svayamvara）。她歷聖地與仙居，心有所定：薩蒂凡，盲眼流放王達優摩陀申之子，居林中貧困。彼俊美、孝謹——而命定將死。神諭：天界仙人那羅陀適在座，宣示預言，故事之鐘由此撥動：薩蒂凡德行冠世，然有一缺陷——他將於一年內死去。父懇求；女之回答是故事的樞紐與其教義：『我已擇定，無論其壽長壽促；既擇，不再擇。』一年之死乃命運之缺陷，非其人之缺陷。婚禮在預言成立之下舉行，薩維特里著粗衣至仙居，侍奉盲眼翁姑。守夜：薩維特里向內數日。期前四日始立齋；翁欲勸阻；她以神學作答——誓願已持，智者知其所將至。劫日，她求得許可與夫同入林中。伐木、昏厥，枕於她膝。隨即她見到他：頭戴暗冠、手持繩索之人，立於林間如主。是閻摩。他抽出薩蒂凡之魂——如拇指般小——繫之，轉向南往亡者之城。決鬥：薩維特里隨行。閻摩三令其返；三留，其言辭——論正法、論與義者同行、論隨夫之功——令死神自認辯不過。他為使其離去而賜恩諾：翁之眼與王國復得；父得百子；己得百子。第三項恩諾正是她步步築成的陷阱：百子需活著的丈夫。閻摩受己諾所縛，一笑斷繩：『汝夫將活。』薩蒂凡如從睡中醒來；流放之家時運逆轉；仙人之預言非為武力所破，而為一位妻子的堅貞——以恰當的時機與措辭——所破。功能：此篇為貞婦理想之憲章——貞婦之德具有真實的宇宙效力——亦為 Vat-Savitri 齋戒的儀式文本：婦女齋戒、於榕樹繫線、重述薩維特里的辯論以為夫爭命。室利阿羅頻多以此構築其史詩《薩維特里》；比較讀者置之於俄耳甫斯（為妻下行而失敗）之旁——此處下行被拒絕，歌所不能者，言辭得之。

functions: Charter of the pativrata ideal - wifely constancy with cosmological efficacy
Ritual text of Vat-Savitri vrata (annual fast for husbands' longevity)
Model of argumentative devotion: boons won by speech, not force
Narrative refutation of fatalism - prophecy beaten by timing and wording

variants.summary: The inverse case: the husband descends for a wife and fails by looking back; Savitri, the wife who follows death, succeeds by never turning back and by out-talking the lord of the dead.

title.en: The Birth of Skanda, the Six-Headed War God
title.zh: 六首戰神塞建陀之誕生

region.en: Saravana reed-beds of the Ganges (symbolic pin in the Himalayan foothills)
region.zh: 恆河薩羅伐那葦叢（象徵性定位於喜馬拉雅山麓）

texts.period: Mahabharata, Vana Parva (Skanda's birth sections), composition layers c. 400 BCE-400 CE (Ganguli translation, 1883-96)

source.work: The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, trans. K. M. Ganguli (1883-96), Vana Parva, the birth and consecration of Skanda

summary.en: The gods are losing to Taraka's demon armies - only a son of Shiva can kill him, but Shiva has withdrawn into yoga. Agni, sent to kindle Shiva's seed, carries it away glowing like molten gold; the Ganga receives it, six reed-nurturing mothers nurse the child, and Skanda rises with six faces to drink from all six at once. On the day he is born, he becomes general of the gods.
summary.zh: 諸神屢敗於達羅迦魔軍——唯濕婆之子能誅之，而濕婆已退入瑜伽。阿耆尼受命燃起濕婆之種，攜之而去，光如熔金；恆河承之，六位哺乳的母親撫育此子，塞建陀生而六首，得同時吮六乳。誕生之日，即被立為諸神之統帥。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition: Skanda-Kartikeya-Murugan worship is major in South India (Murugan temples, Skanda Shashthi festival). Classified 'myth'.

passages.text: The demon Taraka's boon made him nearly immortal: only a son of Shiva could kill him, and Shiva, in grief for Sati, had renounced the world for yogic seclusion. The gods, pressed hard in battle, went to Agni the fire-god, who entered Shiva's presence and received the god's seed, blazing like a second sun; unable to bear it, Agni carried it away to the Ganga, who bore it in her waters.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Skanda sections (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

passages.text: The seed blazed in the river until the water grew hot; the reed-beds of the Saravana gleamed as if on fire. A child was born there among the reeds, beautiful, golden, with six faces; the six Krittika mothers, star-wives who had come to wash, each claimed him, each offered her breast - and the child grew six faces and drank from all six at once, so no mother was refused. He was therefore Kartikeya, of the Krittikas, and Skanda, of the reeds.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Skanda sections (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

passages.text: On the day of his birth the boy grew to youth; on that day the gods consecrated him general of their armies. He was armed, anointed, and seated on the assembled gods' lap in turn; he marshaled the hosts, took the cock standard and the peacock that had fought at his side, and led the army against Taraka's demons - the war the boon had reserved for him, won on the day he learned to walk.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Skanda sections (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: Kisari Mohan Ganguli, The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, 1883-96 (public domain); modern: J. A. B. van Buitenen, The Mahabharata, vol. 3, University of Chicago Press, 1975

narrative.en:
The birth of Skanda (Kartikeya, in the Tamil south Murugan) in the Vana Parva is one of the great miraculous-birth narratives of world mythology - a war god born full-armed and six-headed, made general of the gods on the day of his birth.

The problem the story solves is a theological knot. The demon Taraka's boon (from Brahma) makes him effectively unconquerable: only the son of Shiva may kill him. But Shiva - grief-mad since the death of Sati, his first wife - has renounced the world and sits in yogic seclusion, generating no lineage and answering no petitions. The gods' dilemma is Shiva's own withdrawal: the weapon exists, but the smith will not strike.

The delivery system is Agni. Sent (in some versions by the other gods, in some by Shiva's own consent) to receive the god's seed, Agni enters Shiva's presence at the moment the seed falls - blazing, the text says, like molten gold, like a second sun - and cannot hold it. He carries it to the Ganga, who bears it in her waters; the river grows hot; the reed-beds (saravana, 'the reeds') shine as though on fire. A child is born among the reeds: golden, beautiful, with six faces.

The six mothers: the Krittikas - star-wives of the seven seers in one telling, the Pleiades in another - had come to the river to bathe; each lays claim to the marvelous child and each offers her breast. The child's answer is the birth of his iconography: he sprouts six faces and drinks from all six mothers at once, so that no one is refused and every claim is honored. He is thus Kartikeya ('of the Krittikas') and Skanda ('of the reeds'), and in later iconography rides a peacock, carries a lance, and bears the cock-banner.

Consecration and war: the epic compresses childhood to a single day - on the day of his birth he grows to youth; the gods assemble and consecrate him senapati, general of the divine armies; Indra's jealousy flares and is pacified by an embrace (in the epic's comic aside, Indra strikes the newborn with his thunderbolt and the boy simply grows another body - and Indra, terrified, becomes his devotee). Skanda marshals the hosts, and the war that only he could win is won - Taraka's armies broken, the boon fulfilled, the cosmos re-ordered by an infant-day-old commander.

Function: the myth is a ritual charter of great consequence. It grounds Skanda's cult (huge in the Tamil south, where Murugan is lord of the hills and of youth and war), the Skanda Shashthi festival re-enacting his victory, and the iconic 'six mothers' theology that makes the Pleiades a nursing constellation. It also exemplifies the tradition's birth-miracle pattern: the seed travels (fire to river to reeds), the child is nursed by many mothers, and maturity arrives with cosmic speed. Compared with other miraculous-birth cluster members - Horus in the reeds of the Nile, Sargon in the reeds of a river - the shared grammar (dangerous child, water-birth, reed-cradle, immediate destiny) is unmistakable, but here the child's destiny is martial command rather than royal survival.
narrative.zh: 大森林篇中塞建陀（迦爾底克耶；南印度稱穆盧甘）之誕生是世界神話中最偉大的奇蹟誕生敘事之一——一位滿懷武備、六首而在誕生日即被立為諸神統帥的戰神。故事所解的神學結：魔王達羅迦之恩諭（得自梵天）使其近乎不可征服：唯濕婆之子可誅之。而濕婆——自其首妻薩提死後哀慟——已棄世入瑜伽深定，不生後嗣，不應請求。諸神的困境正是濕婆自身的隱退：武器存在，而鑄者不擊。遞送系統是阿耆尼。受命（或由諸神、或由濕婆許可）承接收神之種，阿耆尼入於濕婆之前，於種子落下之刻——其熾然如熔金、如第二太陽——不能持之。他攜之至恆河，恆河以其水承之；河水轉熱；葦叢（saravana，『葦』）熠然如焚。葦叢中生一子：金色、俊美、六首。六母：克里蒂迦（一說七仙人之星妻，一說昴星團）來河中沐浴；各欲認領此奇童，各奉其乳。孩童的回答即是其圖像學之誕生：他生出六面，同時吮六母之乳，無一被拒，每一主張皆得成全。故其名迦爾底克耶（『克里蒂迦之子』）與塞建陀（『葦中所生』）；後世圖像中騎孔雀、持長矛、立雞旗。授職與戰爭：史詩將童年壓縮為一日——誕生之日即長成青年；諸神集會，立其為元帥（senapati）；因陀羅之妒爆發而後平息（史詩的滑稽旁注：因陀羅以雷杵擊新生之嬰，孩童僅另生一身——因陀羅大懼，轉為其信徒）。塞建陀整頓神軍，唯他能贏的戰爭遂被贏得——達羅迦之軍潰，恩諭應驗，宇宙由一位出生未滿一日的統帥重整。功能：此神話是影響深遠的儀式憲章。它奠定塞建陀崇拜（南泰米爾尤盛，穆盧甘為山嶽、青春與戰爭之主）、重演其勝利的塞建陀六日節（Skanda Shashthi），以及『六母』神學——昴星團由此成為哺乳星座。它亦示範該傳統的誕生奇蹟模式：種子旅行（火至河至葦）、多母哺乳、成熟以宇宙速度降臨。與其他奇蹟誕生母題群成員相比——尼羅河葦中的荷魯斯、河中葦籃裡的薩爾貢——共享語法（危險之童、水生、葖搖籃、即刻命運）顯而易見，但此處孩童的命運是統軍而非王儲之存續。

functions: Miraculous-birth charter: seed travels by fire, river and reeds; six mothers nurse one child
Cultic foundation of Skanda-Kartikeya-Murugan worship and the Skanda Shashthi festival
Theology of the Pleiades as nursing constellation (the Krittikas)
Resolution myth: a boon-proof demon killed by the one son the boon excluded

title.en: Yudhishthira's Last Journey: The Dog at Heaven's Gate
title.zh: 堅戰的末程：天門前的犬

region.en: Mount Meru, path of ascent (symbolic pin at Kailash)
region.zh: 彌樓山登天之路（象徵性定位於凱拉什）

texts.period: Mahabharata, Mahaprasthanika and Svargarohana Parvas, composition layers c. 400 BCE-400 CE (Ganguli translation, 1883-96)

source.work: The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, trans. K. M. Ganguli (1883-96), Svargarohana Parva, Yudhishthira's ascent with the dog

summary.en: After the war and Krishna's passing, the five Pandavas and Draupadi walk west and north toward Mount Meru, dropping one by one as their particular sins are paid. Only Yudhishthira, the just, reaches heaven's gate in his body - with a stray dog that has followed him. Indra offers heaven without the dog; Yudhishthira refuses; the dog turns out to be Dharma, his father, testing him - and the gate opens.
summary.zh: 大戰之後、克里希那離世之際，般度五子與黑公主向西向北朝彌樓山而行，各因其私罪逐一倒下。唯堅戰——行義者——肉身抵達天門，伴有一路跟隨的流浪犬。因陀羅許其入天而棄犬；堅戰拒之；犬化為正法——其父——考驗而成，天門乃開。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition (epic recitation, bhakti readings). Classified 'myth'.

passages.text: When word came of Krishna's death and the drowning of his clan, Yudhishthira resolved that the time of departure had come. The five brothers and Draupadi, adorned and fasting, turned from the city and walked toward the great mountain, the road of renunciation; a stray dog joined them and walked behind Yudhishthira, and the age's princes went as beggars toward Meru.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Mahaprasthanika Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

passages.text: One by one they fell. Draupadi fell first, and Yudhishthira, without turning aside, named her fault - she leaned toward Arjuna. Sahadeva fell for vanity of wisdom, Nakula for pride in beauty, Arjuna for his boast, Bhima for his gluttony; each fell, and Yudhishthira walked on, grief and fault acknowledged, until only he and the dog climbed the peak.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Mahaprasthanika Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

passages.text: At the gate Indra came down to meet him and offered heaven in his chariot - but without the dog. Yudhishthira asked: what of my brothers and Draupadi? They are already there, said Indra - they went before you. Then, refusing heaven that excludes a creature that trusted him, Yudhishthira answered: the dog has followed me through the wilds; I will not abandon one who seeks my protection, not for the worlds themselves. A rescue of the helpless, he said, outcounts even heaven.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Svargarohana Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

passages.text: At that the dog took the form of Dharma, god of justice, Yudhishthira's own divine father, and blessed him: thou hast renounced the carriage of heaven for a dog's companionship; no man on earth was ever thy equal in righteousness. Then Yudhishthira was carried up in glory - but the epic is not done: shown the heaven of his enemies, and his brothers in a hell being purified of a last sin, he refuses heaven that his loved ones cannot share, until hell and heaven are both remitted and the truth of the age's violence is paid in full.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Svargarohana Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: Kisari Mohan Ganguli, The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, 1883-96 (public domain); modern: J. A. B. van Buitenen, The Mahabharata, vols. 6-7 (Chicago, incomplete)

narrative.en:
The Mahaprasthanika ('great departure') and Svargarohana ('ascent to heaven') Parvas are the Mahabharata's coda: after the war's desolation, Krishna's death, and the drowning of the Yadavas, the epic's heroes leave the world on foot - and the tradition's theology is tested at heaven's gate.

The departure: word arrives of Krishna's passing. Yudhishthira judges the age's work complete: 'the time has come for us to depart'. The five brothers and Draupadi, adorned like sacrificial victors and fasting, walk out of Hastinapura toward the west and north, the road of renunciation toward Mount Meru. A stray dog joins them - unbidden, unprompted - and attaches itself to Yudhishthira.

The falls: one by one they drop on the road, each fall explained by Yudhishthira in a single unturned sentence - the epic's harshest audit. Draupadi falls because she favored Arjuna in her heart; Sahadeva for vanity of wisdom; Nakula for pride in beauty; Arjuna for his boast (that he could consume his enemies in a day); Bhima for his gluttony. The just king alone keeps walking - his own flaw (the gambling, the lie that felled Drona) paid long before - until only he and the dog stand on the peak, and the gate of heaven shines before them.

The gate: Indra descends in his chariot and offers Yudhishthira heaven in his body. Yudhishthira asks for his brothers and Draupadi - told they are already there. Then the offer's condition: not the dog. A dog may not enter heaven, Indra says; cast it off and ascend. Yudhishthira's refusal is the epic's last teaching: the dog followed him through the wilds for its own reasons and now seeks his protection; to abandon a creature that has sought shelter is a sin no heaven could outweigh - 'I would not do such a thing for the sake of the three worlds, let alone heaven'. (The scene's genealogy is visible: it is a Vedic-test echo - in the Rigveda's Yama hymns the two four-eyed dogs guard the path of the dead; here the dog becomes the gate's own examiner.)

The theophany: at the refusal, the dog assumes the form of Dharma - the god of justice, Yudhishthira's own divine father - and reveals that the whole ascent was his test: 'thou hast renounced the carriage of heaven for a dog's companionship; no man on earth was ever thy equal in righteousness.' Yudhishthira is borne up in splendor.

But the epic's real brilliance is the twist that follows: shown around heaven, Yudhishthira finds his enemies honored (Duryodhana, radiant, among the gods) and his own brothers and Draupadi undergoing a brief hell, purifying the last sin - the lie and the war's guilt. Yudhishthira refuses to stay in a heaven built on such arrangements, demands to share their hell, and his renunciation of heaven itself completes the purification: hell and heaven both are remitted, and the age's violence is paid in full. The poem ends where its ethics began - with a king who will not accept a reward that costs others their share.

Function: the closing parvas are the epic's theodicy and its ethics' final exam; the dog-test became proverbial (dharma outcounts heaven), and the scene is retold in bhakti sermons as the model of compassion that outranks reward.
narrative.zh: 『大去篇』（Mahaprasthanika）與『登天篇』（Svargarohana）是摩訶婆羅多的尾聲：大戰之後、克里希那之死、雅度族之溺，史詩的英雄們徒步離世——傳統的神學在天門前受試。離去：克里希那逝去的消息傳到。堅戰斷定時機已至：『我們該啟程了。』五兄弟與黑公主如祭祀勝利者般飾身、持齋，步出象城向西向北，往彌樓山而行出離之路。一隻流浪犬不請自來，附於堅戰身後。倒下：他們一個個在路上倒下，每一次跌倒皆由堅戰以一句不回頭的話解釋——史詩最嚴厲的審計。黑公主因心偏阿周那而倒；無種因智慧之傲；偕天因美貌之驕；阿周那因誇言（一日盡殲敵軍）；怖軍因饕餮。唯義王繼續前行——他自身的過失（賭局、誅德羅納之謊）早已償清——直到唯他與犬立於峰頂，天門在眼前生輝。天門：因陀羅乘車而降，許堅戰肉身升天。堅戰求其兄弟與黑公主——被告知他們已先至。隨後是條件：犬不可入。因陀羅言：犬不得進天；棄之而升。堅戰的拒絕是史詩的最後一課：犬循其自身之由隨我穿過荒野，此刻尋我庇護；拋棄尋求庇護之生靈是任何天國都抵不過的罪——『為三界我亦不為此，何况天國』。（此景的譜系清晰可見：吠陀閻摩頌中守亡者之路的是雙四眼犬；此處犬成為門的考官本身。）神顯：拒絕之際，犬化為正法之神——堅戰的神性之父——揭示整段上升皆是其試：『汝為犬伴而棄天車；地上無人於義行汝之比。』堅戰於光榮中被舉起。然史詩真正的妙筆在其後的轉折：參觀天國時，堅戰發現其仇敵受尊（難敵光燦燦地立於諸神之中），而自己的兄弟與黑公主正於短暫的地獄中受煉，以淨最後之罪——謊言與戰爭之責。堅戰拒絕居於如此安排的天國，求與他們同下地獄；他對天國自身的棄絕完成了淨化：地獄與天國皆得釋免，時代的暴力償清。詩在其倫理開始處收尾——以一位不肯接受以他人之份為代價的賞賜的王。功能：末二篇是史詩的神義論與其倫理的終考；犬試成為諺語（正法勝於天國），此景在奉愛佈道中被重述為慈悲高於賞賜的典範。

functions: Final ethics of the epic: compassion outranks heaven's reward (the dog test)
Theodicy of the war - sin paid on the road, in hell, and by refusing heaven
Death-walk rite of renunciation (pravrajya) enacted by the heroes
Model for bhakti preaching on protection of the helpless

texts.period: Ramayana of Valmiki, oldest strata c. 2nd c. BCE-2nd c. CE (Griffith translation, 1870-74)

source.work: The Ramayan of Valmiki, trans. Ralph T. H. Griffith (1870-74), Yuddha Kanda (Book VI), the fire trial of Sita

summary.en: Ravana is dead; Rama is reunited with Sita before the armies - and coldly tells her to go where she will, for honor dwells not with a woman who has lived in another's house. Sita bids Lakshmana build a pyre and enters the fire, praying to be proof of her faithfulness. Agni, the fire god himself, rises from the flames holding her unharmed - and gives her back, declaring her purity before the assembled hosts.
summary.zh: 羅波那已死；羅摩與悉多於兩軍之前重聚——卻冷言令其自去，言貞操不居於曾居他人之宅的女子。悉多命羅什曼那築火堆，投身入火，祈以火為其貞信之證。火神阿耆尼親自自焰中持不傷之悉多而起，於會眾之前宣告其貞潔，將她交還。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition and politically contested narrative (the agni-pariksha is debated in contemporary India; Uttara Kanda variants exist). Classified 'myth'.

passages.text: Rama, having slain Ravana and received back his wife, stood before the hosts and spoke words colder than the battlefield: I have fought for honor, not desire; Sita has lived in another's house; let her go where she will - I take her back only as a man takes back his name, cleansed of suspicion.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ramayana, Yuddha Kanda, the fire trial (Griffith 1870-74); not verbatim.

passages.text: Sita, wounded, answered that she had not strayed in thought; and to the assembled army she made her vow: if my heart has never left my lord, then let the fire, witness of all, protect me. She ordered Lakshmana: build the pyre. Lakshmana, anguished, looked to Rama, who nodded - and the pyre was raised, and Sita, circling her lord three times, mounted it before the world.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ramayana, Yuddha Kanda, the fire trial (Griffith 1870-74); not verbatim.

passages.text: She entered the flames as into the presence of the gods; the fire burned bright around her, and the armies groaned - mothers of the monkeys wept, Rakshasa women lamented. Then the earth seemed to open: from the blazing pyre rose Agni himself, the fire-god in human form, red-lit, bearing Sita unharmed upon his hands, her garments white, her body cool as if she walked in moonlight - and with a voice like a conch he proclaimed her purity before gods and men.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ramayana, Yuddha Kanda, the fire trial (Griffith 1870-74); not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: Ralph T. H. Griffith, The Ramayan of Valmiki, Benares, 1870-74 (public domain); modern critical: Robert P. Goldman et al., The Ramayana of Valmiki, vol. VI, Princeton University Press, 2017

narrative.en:
The agni-pariksha - Sita's trial by fire at the close of the Lanka war - is the Ramayana's most theologically charged scene and, in modern India, its most politically debated one.

The situation: Ravana is slain. Vibhishana brings Sita from the Ashoka grove to her husband, veiled and dishevelled after months of captivity, surrounded by the victorious armies of monkeys, bears and rakshasa defectors. The reunion the whole war has aimed at begins - and Rama stops it with a speech of public humiliation: he fought for honor and the family's name, not for desire; a woman who has dwelt in another man's house cannot be received by him without suspicion; let her go wherever she pleases - to Lakshmana, to Bharata, to Shatrughna, to the forest, or to Ravana's kin. The victory speech is a rejection.

Sita's response defines her. She has endured abduction, captivity, threats, the surveillance of demonesses - and now this. She answers first with the record of her faithfulness (in thought she never left him), then does the unthinkable: she orders Lakshmana to build a pyre. Her logic is stated as a vow to the assembled world: 'if my heart has never strayed from Rama, let the fire, witness of all deeds, protect me.' Lakshmana - the brother who never questioned Rama - hesitates, looks to Rama for instruction, and Rama's silent assent seals the horror. Sita circles her lord three times with folded hands, prays to Agni, and mounts the pyre as the two armies watch in tears.

The fire answers. From the blazing pyre the fire-god Agni himself rises in person - the text makes him a visible being, red-lit, human-formed - carrying Sita unharmed, her body cool, her garments unsinged, and proclaims to gods and men that she is pure: no sin touches her, in thought, word or deed; she was preserved through captivity as a pearl is kept in a shell. Rama receives her back - the text notes pointedly that he then claims he acted only to demonstrate her purity to the world, a claim the poem leaves sitting awkwardly beside the cruelty of the speech that began it.

Function and afterlife: in the epic's own theology, the trial authenticates Sita as the earth-daughter whose purity is cosmically guaranteed; fire is the Vedic witness of oaths, and here the witness speaks. But the scene's authority has always been contested inside the tradition: the Ramcharitmanas softens it; regional folk tellings often refuse it outright (Sita refuses the test, or Rama refuses to ask it); the Jain Paumacariya and some Tamil tellings remove the trial entirely; and modern India has turned the episode into a public argument about the treatment of women and the reading of scripture (Supreme Court hearings in the 1980s-90s turned on Sita's and Draupadi's trials as cultural arguments). The Uttara Kanda's later exile of Sita - despite the trial's verdict - makes the poem's own conclusion a second, crueler trial; the tradition has never fully reconciled the two.

Comparatively, the scene belongs to the ordeal-by-fire cluster (like the medieval ordeals of Europe, and the suttee rhetoric it would later be contaminated by) - but here the ordeal is divine theater: the god of fire himself is the judge, and the accused is vindicated. The record keeps both the vindication and the cruelty in view.
narrative.zh: 火證（agni-pariksha）——楞伽之戰尾聲悉多的火中試煉——是《羅摩衍那》神學上最沉重的一幕，在現代印度也是政治上爭論最烈的一幕。情境：羅波那已誅。維毗沙那自無憂樹林帶出歷經數月囚禁、蒙塵披髮的悉多，交給其夫，四周環繞著猴、熊與投誠羅剎的勝利大軍。整場戰爭所指向的重聚開始——而羅摩以一場公開羞辱的言辭止住它：我為榮譽與家族之名而戰，非為欲；曾居他人之宅的女子，我不能無疑地接納；隨其所欲而去——去羅什曼那處、婆羅多處、沙陀魯那處、去森林、去羅波那親族處。勝利之辭成為拒絕。悉多的回應定義了她。她受過擄掠、囚禁、威脅、羅剎女的監視——如今又是這個。她先陳述其貞信之記錄（心未曾離），繼而做出不可思議之事：命羅什曼那築火堆。其邏輯以向天下之誓表述：『若我心未曾離羅摩，願火——萬行之見證——護我。』羅什曼那——那位從不質疑兄長的弟弟——遲疑，望向羅摩求示；羅摩的默許封存了這場恐怖。悉多合掌繞夫三匝，祈於阿耆尼，於兩軍垂淚注視之下登上火堆。火作出回答。自熊熊火堆中火神阿耆尼親自升起——經文使其成為可見之存在，紅光人形——手持不傷之悉多，其身涼爽，衣無燎痕，並向諸神與世人宣告其純潔：思、言、行皆無罪；她於囚禁中被保全，如貝中之珠。羅摩復接納她——經文刻意記下他隨即宣稱此舉只為向世界昭示其貞潔——此說與開場那場殘酷言辭並置時顯得突兀，而詩篇並未解決這一張力。功能與後續：在史詩自身的神學中，此試驗認證悉多為大地之女、其貞潔具宇宙保證；火是吠陀誓言的見證者，而在此見證者開口。然而此景的權威在傳統內部始終有爭議：《羅摩功行錄》予以柔化；各地民間講述常直接拒絕（悉多拒試，或羅摩拒問）；耆那教《缽摩迦哩耶》與若干泰米爾講述整體移除此試；現代印度更將此幕轉為關於婦女處境與經典詮釋的公共論辯（1980-90年代最高法院聽證曾以悉多與黑公主之試為文化論據）。後篇（Uttara Kanda）中悉多縱經火證仍遭放逐——使詩篇自身的結論成為第二場、更殘酷的試煉；傳統從未完全調和二者。比較地看，此景屬於火審母題群（如歐洲中世紀火審，及其後被寡婦殉葬論述所污染的語境）——但此處神判是神聖劇場：火神親自為法官，被告獲平反。本錄同時保留平反與殘酷兩面。

functions: Ordeal theology: fire as Vedic witness of oaths, speaking its verdict
Authentication of Sita's purity as earth-daughter before the world
Most debated scene of the epic - charter of contested gender norms
Ritual resonance in Sita-related vows and folk retellings that refuse or soften the trial

variants.name: Ramcharitmanas of Tulsidas (Awadhi, 1574)
variants.summary: Softens the trial: Rama's speech is read as lila (divine play), the fire-trial staged as a spectacle of devotion rather than suspicion, and Sita's divinity foregrounded.

variants.name: Paumacariya of Vimalasuri (Jain, c. 3rd-5th c. CE)
variants.summary: Removes the trial entirely; Ravana is noble and Sita untested - the ideology reworked through Jain vows and karma, with Lakshmana as the slayer of Ravana.

variants.name: Folk refusals of the trial
variants.text_tradition: Regional oral tellings (e.g. Telugu, Bengali traditions)
variants.summary: In many village tellings Sita refuses to enter the fire, or Rama withdraws the demand; the trial is the most locally variable scene of the whole poem.

texts.sensitivity_guidance: The agni-pariksha is ritually recited and politically contested (courts, public debate). Quote public-domain translations; attribute kanda and sarga; present the trial as the tradition's own contested scene, noting folk and Jain refusals; do not present the ordeal as normative or as historical fact.
